index.whyChooseTitle: Why Choose the OKLCH Color Space?
index.whyChooseBody: The OKLCH color space (Oklab Lightness, Chroma, Hue) solves the historic flaws of RGB and HSL. In HSL, blue and yellow with 50% lightness appear vastly different in perceived brightness to human eyes. OKLCH guarantees perceptual uniformity: 60% lightness looks equally bright regardless of hue angle, making accessible UI themes, dark modes, and dynamic color systems predictable and effortless.
index.howToTitle: How to Pick and Export Colors
index.step1Body: Move the sliders to set your base hue and lightness. The dynamic slider tracks render real-time color spectra along each individual axis.
index.step2Body: Click Add to Cart to assign your color to a semantic token role (--color-trusty-button-500). Colors auto-slot into shade steps 50 to 950.
index.step3Body: Open the Export page to copy a ready-to-use @theme block or download a custom CSS variable stylesheet with VS Code inline color decorators.
index.gotchasTitle: Important Gotchas: Gamut Clipping & Browser Fallbacks
index.gotcha1: Display-P3 Gamut: OKLCH can describe colors outside the standard sRGB triangle. On displays that support P3, colors will appear more vivid. On older screens, modern browsers clamp chroma automatically.
index.gotcha2: Lightness Rounding: Lightness in CSS OKLCH can be expressed as a percentage (62%) or decimal (0.62). Both represent identical optical lightness.
index.gotcha3: Tailwind v4 @theme: When exported to Tailwind v4, custom CSS variables prefixed with --color-{role}-{step} instantly become utilities like bg-trusty-button-500.
index.faqSubtitle: Using the badge on the colour canvas? Click it — sRGB, Display-P3 and Clipped each jump to their own answer here.
index.faq1Question: What is the difference between OKLCH and HSL?
index.faq1Answer: HSL distorts perceived brightness: yellow at 50% lightness looks almost white, while blue at 50% lightness looks dark. OKLCH fixes this with mathematically modeled human visual perception, ensuring lightness is uniform regardless of hue.
index.faq2Question: Do all modern browsers support CSS oklch()?
index.faq2Answer: Yes! Chrome 111+, Safari 15.4+, Firefox 113+, and Edge 111+ support oklch() natively, representing over 93% global browser adoption.
index.faq3Question: How does the color cart work?
index.faq3Answer: Whenever you click "Add to Cart" or tap a swatch from our palettes, that exact single color is placed into your chosen UI role (e.g. Primary, Trusty Button, Danger). It automatically slots into the closest shade step (50–950), which you can then preview on real dummy UI components or export to Tailwind v4.
index.faq4Question: What does "sRGB" mean on the gamut badge?
index.faq4Answer: The color fits inside sRGB — the standard gamut that every screen, browser, and CSS color function can display. The badge's green dot means what you see on the canvas is exactly what the copied oklch() value will render: nothing is being clamped, so the swatch is a literal preview of the value.
index.faq5Question: What does "Display-P3" mean on the gamut badge?
index.faq5Answer: The color is more vivid than sRGB can reproduce, but still fits Display-P3 — the wider gamut used by modern phones, laptops, and monitors. Wide-gamut displays show it at full intensity; on older sRGB-only screens the browser gamut-maps it back toward sRGB, so it may look slightly less vivid there. It is a real, usable color — just one that benefits from a P3 display to appreciate fully.
index.faq6Question: What does "Clipped" mean on the gamut badge?
index.faq6Answer: The color is too saturated even for Display-P3, so no current screen can show it as authored — the browser clamps it to the nearest displayable color and the swatch becomes an approximation of your OKLCH values rather than the values themselves. Lower the Chroma slider (its max label shows the sRGB ceiling for that lightness and hue) until the badge reads sRGB or Display-P3 to get a color you can trust.

whatIsOklch.subtitle: OKLCH is a modern cylindrical representation of the Oklab color space designed specifically for human vision. It fixes the mathematical flaws of RGB and HSL by ensuring that identical numerical lightness values look equally bright across all hues.
whatIsOklch.whatIsBody1: OKLCH is a perceptually uniform color space that describes colors using three values: Lightness (L), Chroma (C), and Hue (H). Unlike RGB and HSL, OKLCH is designed to match human color perception — equal changes in its numerical values produce equal changes in perceived color. This makes it ideal for creating accessible, consistent color systems in CSS.
whatIsOklch.whatIsBody2: OKLCH is the cylindrical form of the Oklab color space, standardized in CSS Color Module Level 4. It is supported by all modern browsers and is the default color space for Tailwind CSS v4's entire palette.
whatIsOklch.standsForBody: OKLCH stands for Oklab Lightness, Chroma, Hue. The "OK" comes from Oklab, the color space created by Björn Ottosson in 2020. Oklab itself is named after the LMS cone response model it uses (L, M, S), with "Ok" indicating that it is a perceptually uniform improvement over earlier models.
whatIsOklch.lBody: 0% (black) to 100% (white). Perceptual brightness that matches human vision.
whatIsOklch.cBody: Color intensity. 0 is neutral gray; higher values are more vivid. Maximum ~0.4.
whatIsOklch.hBody: Color angle on the 360° wheel. 0° is magenta, 140° is green, 255° is blue.
whatIsOklch.howWorksBody1: OKLCH works by transforming colors through a perceptually uniform color space. The L (Lightness) axis runs from black to white and is designed so that equal numerical steps look equally bright. The C (Chroma) axis measures color intensity as distance from the gray center. The H (Hue) axis is a circle of color angles. Together they form a cylinder: L is the vertical axis, C is the radius, and H is the angle around the center.
whatIsOklch.howWorksBody2: The key property is perceptual uniformity: a color at 50% lightness looks equally bright whether it is red, blue, or yellow. This is not true of HSL, where 50% lightness yellow looks almost white and 50% lightness blue looks very dark.
whatIsOklch.diagramBody: The OKLCH color space can be visualized as a cylinder. Lightness (L) runs vertically from black (0%) at the bottom to white (100%) at the top. Chroma (C) is the radial distance from the center axis — the center is neutral gray, and the outer edge is the most vivid color possible at that lightness. Hue (H) is the angle around the cylinder.
whatIsOklch.diagramCaption: The OKLCH cylinder: Lightness (L) is the vertical axis, Chroma (C) is the radial distance from center, and Hue (H) is the angle around the cylinder.
whatIsOklch.cssBody: OKLCH is used in CSS via the oklch() function. The syntax is oklch(L C H) where L is lightness (0% to 100%), C is chroma (0 to 0.4), and H is hue (0 to 360). An optional alpha value can be added after a slash: oklch(0.7 0.15 250 / 50%).
whatIsOklch.cssSyntaxLabel: oklch(Lightness Chroma Hue [/ Alpha])
whatIsOklch.basicSyntaxCode:
color: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8);
color: oklch(0.623 0.188 259.8); /* same, decimal form */

whatIsOklch.whyMovedTitle: Why Designers Moved from RGB and HSL
whatIsOklch.whyMovedBody: HSL's lightness is not perceptually uniform. Pure yellow (hsl(60, 100%, 50%)) and pure blue (hsl(240, 100%, 50%)) both claim 50% lightness, but the human eye perceives yellow as overwhelmingly bright and blue as very dark. OKLCH fixes this: at 70% lightness, yellow and blue look equally bright.
whatIsOklch.hslNote: Notice how blinding yellow is compared to blue despite having the exact same "50% lightness" parameter.
whatIsOklch.oklchNote: In OKLCH, 70% lightness produces identical optical luminance across any hue angle.
whatIsOklch.benefit1: Predictable palettes: Equal lightness steps look equally spaced, making 50-950 scales trivial to generate.
whatIsOklch.benefit2: Accessibility: Contrast ratios are more predictable because lightness is perceptually uniform.
whatIsOklch.benefit3: Wide gamut: OKLCH can describe Display-P3 colors that HSL cannot reach.
whatIsOklch.benefit4: Smooth gradients: Interpolating in OKLCH avoids the muddy midtones that RGB interpolation produces.
whatIsOklch.browserSupportBody1: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature, meaning it is widely available across all modern browsers. According to MDN, it has been available across browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively.
whatIsOklch.browserSupportBody2: For older browsers that do not support OKLCH, use the progressive enhancement pattern: declare a HEX or RGB fallback first, then override with OKLCH. Browsers that do not understand OKLCH will simply ignore the second declaration and use the fallback.
whatIsOklch.tailwindTitle: When did Tailwind CSS start using OKLCH?
whatIsOklch.tailwindBody1: Tailwind CSS v4.0, released on January 22, 2025, moved its entire default color palette from RGB to OKLCH. The v4.0 release notes state: "We've upgraded the entire default color palette from rgb to oklch, taking advantage of the wider gamut to make the colors more vivid in places where we were previously limited by the sRGB color space."
whatIsOklch.tailwindBody2: This means every color in Tailwind's default palette — from red-500 to blue-600 — is now defined in OKLCH. Custom colors defined in the @theme block also use OKLCH by default.

whatIsOklch.faq2Question: Do all modern browsers support CSS oklch()?
whatIsOklch.faq2Answer: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively.
whatIsOklch.faq3Question: Can I use OKLCH in Tailwind CSS v4?
whatIsOklch.faq3Answer: Yes. Tailwind v4 uses OKLCH for its entire default palette. Define custom colors in your @theme block using --color-{name}: oklch(...) and Tailwind generates utilities automatically.
whatIsOklch.faq4Question: What happens when an OKLCH color is out of sRGB gamut?
whatIsOklch.faq4Answer: On sRGB displays, the browser automatically tone-maps the color to the nearest displayable equivalent. On wide-gamut Display-P3 monitors, the color appears more vivid. Use the progressive enhancement pattern to provide a HEX fallback for older browsers.
whatIsOklch.faq5Question: Is OKLCH the same as OKLab?
whatIsOklch.faq5Answer: OKLCH is the cylindrical form of OKLab. OKLab uses Cartesian coordinates (L, a, b) while OKLCH uses cylindrical coordinates (L, C, H). They describe the same color space — OKLCH is simply more intuitive for most design tasks.

hexToOklch.subtitle: Convert 3-digit, 6-digit, or 8-digit hexadecimal colors into standard CSS oklch() notation with perceptual accuracy and live gamut detection.
hexToOklch.whyTitle: Why Convert HEX Colors to OKLCH?
hexToOklch.whyBody: Hexadecimal color codes (#RRGGBB) have served the web for decades, but they are tied to device-dependent sRGB color spaces. When building dynamic design systems, tweaking the brightness of a HEX color requires complex, inaccurate math. In contrast, OKLCH separates lightness, chroma, and hue into independent parameters: you can change lightness from 40% to 80% without affecting the chromatic purity or shifting the hue angle.
hexToOklch.howTitle: How to Convert HEX to OKLCH
hexToOklch.step1: Type or paste any HEX value (e.g. #3b82f6 or with alpha #3b82f680) into the input field above.
hexToOklch.step2: Our engine immediately calculates the exact perceptual Lightness (L), Chroma (C), and Hue (H).
hexToOklch.step3: Click Copy to copy the output or + Cart to store this token into your role collection.
hexToOklch.mathPath: The math path: HEX → sRGB (0-255) → linear RGB (gamma decode) → Oklab (LMS cone response matrices) → OKLCH (cylindrical transform). The result is a perceptually uniform color where equal lightness values look equally bright across all hues.

hexToOklch.cssIntro: Use the HEX value as a fallback for older browsers, then override with OKLCH for modern browsers:
hexToOklch.gamutTitle: Gamut Note: HEX is Always sRGB-Safe
hexToOklch.gamutSrgbItem: sRGB Gamut Bounds: Because all standard HEX codes exist inside sRGB, converting from HEX to OKLCH is always 100% gamut-safe and will never produce out-of-gamut clipping warnings.
hexToOklch.gamutAlphaItem: 8-Digit Alpha Support: If you input an 8-character HEX code (e.g. #3b82f6cc), the alpha channel is converted into a standard slash parameter: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.80).
hexToOklch.gamutP3Item: Display-P3 Monitors: On wide-gamut displays, the same OKLCH value may appear more vivid than the original HEX, because OKLCH can describe colors beyond the sRGB triangle. The browser handles this automatically.
hexToOklch.faq1Q: Are HEX to OKLCH conversions reversible without loss?
hexToOklch.faq1A: Yes. Because sRGB is a mathematical subset of OKLCH, converting a HEX value into OKLCH and then back to HEX yields the exact original 6-digit hexadecimal code. The round-trip is lossless for all sRGB colors.
hexToOklch.faq2Q: Can I paste 3-digit shorthand HEX codes?
hexToOklch.faq2A: Yes! Our converter natively parses shorthand codes like #fff or #f00 and expands them correctly. Each digit is duplicated (#f00 → #ff0000) before conversion.
hexToOklch.faq3Q: What is the difference between OKLCH and HEX?
hexToOklch.faq3A: HEX is a device-dependent sRGB notation that mixes red, green, and blue channels. OKLCH is a perceptually uniform color space that separates lightness, chroma, and hue — making it far easier to create accessible, consistent color systems.
hexToOklch.faq4Q: Do all modern browsers support CSS oklch()?
hexToOklch.faq4A: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively. See the MDN browser compatibility table for details.
hexToOklch.faq5Q: How do I use OKLCH in Tailwind CSS v4?
hexToOklch.faq5A: Tailwind v4 uses OKLCH for its entire default palette. Define custom colors in your @theme block using --color-{name}: oklch(...) and Tailwind generates utilities like bg-{name} automatically.

oklchToHex.subtitle: Convert CSS oklch() strings into standard 6-digit or 8-digit HEX format with automatic sRGB gamut clamping and wide Display-P3 detection.
oklchToHex.whyBody: While modern browsers and CSS frameworks like Tailwind v4 natively support OKLCH, legacy tools — such as older image software, email templates, or SVG renderers — still demand hexadecimal values. Our converter maps OKLCH values into standard HEX, providing an exact clamped fallback for wide-gamut Display-P3 colors.
oklchToHex.howTitle: How to Convert OKLCH to HEX
oklchToHex.step1: Paste any oklch() value (e.g. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8)) into the input field above.
oklchToHex.step2: Our engine converts the cylindrical OKLCH coordinates back through Oklab to linear RGB, then gamma-encodes to sRGB.
oklchToHex.step3: The result is a 6-digit HEX code (or 8-digit with alpha) that you can copy or save to your cart.
oklchToHex.mathPath: The math path: OKLCH → Oklab (Cartesian) → linear RGB (inverse LMS matrix) → gamma-encoded sRGB → HEX. If the color falls outside sRGB, chroma is clamped to the nearest in-gamut value.
oklchToHex.cssIntro: Ship the HEX fallback first, then override with OKLCH for modern browsers:
oklchToHex.gamutTitle: Gamut Note: What Happens Outside sRGB
oklchToHex.gamutBody: Because HEX is physically confined to sRGB, high-chroma OKLCH colors (such as vibrant cyans or punchy greens with C > 0.22) cannot be rendered accurately in HEX. Our tool calculates the closest possible in-gamut chroma without distorting the perceptual hue angle, ensuring your fallback hex colors look harmonious.
oklchToHex.clampItem: Clamping vs. Display-P3: On a Display-P3 monitor, the original OKLCH color appears more vivid. On an sRGB monitor, the browser automatically tone-maps it. The HEX fallback always represents the sRGB-clamped version.
oklchToHex.alphaItem: Alpha Channel: An OKLCH value with alpha (e.g. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5)) converts to an 8-digit HEX code (e.g. #3b82f680).
oklchToHex.faq1Q: What happens if my OKLCH color is in Display-P3?
oklchToHex.faq1A: If the color exceeds sRGB boundaries, our engine alerts you with a Display-P3 badge and automatically provides the optimal clamped sRGB HEX code as a graceful fallback. The hue and lightness are preserved as closely as possible.
oklchToHex.faq2Q: How do I export HEX fallbacks in CSS?
oklchToHex.faq2A: On our Export page, switch to the "HEX Fallback + OKLCH" tab to generate twin variable lines, ensuring full backward compatibility on legacy browsers.
oklchToHex.faq3Q: Is the OKLCH to HEX conversion lossy?
oklchToHex.faq3A: For sRGB colors, the conversion is lossless — you get back the exact same HEX value. For Display-P3 colors, the conversion to HEX requires clamping to sRGB, which is a lossy step. The OKLCH original remains the source of truth.
oklchToHex.faq4Q: Can I convert OKLCH with alpha to 8-digit HEX?
oklchToHex.faq4A: Yes. An OKLCH value like oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) converts to #3b82f680 — the last two digits represent the alpha channel in hex.
oklchToHex.faq5Q: Why does my HEX color look different on different screens?
oklchToHex.faq5A: HEX values are absolute sRGB colors. On a wide-gamut Display-P3 monitor, the browser may render them more vividly than on a standard sRGB monitor. This is expected behavior — the HEX value itself does not change.

rgbToOklch.subtitle: Convert rgb(r, g, b) and rgba(r, g, b, a) into CSS OKLCH format with live gamut boundary checks.
rgbToOklch.whyBody: RGB mixes red, green, and blue light components, but it is completely non-linear with respect to human vision. Mixing equal parts RGB produces irregular visual steps. By converting into OKLCH, you gain access to linear perceptual lightness, enabling harmonious tints and shades for modern design systems.
rgbToOklch.howTitle: How to Convert RGB to OKLCH
rgbToOklch.step1: Paste any rgb() or rgba() value (e.g. rgb(59, 130, 246)) into the input field above.
rgbToOklch.step2: Our engine normalizes the 0-255 channels to 0-1, applies gamma decoding to get linear RGB, then transforms through the Oklab LMS cone response matrices.
rgbToOklch.step3: The result is a perceptually uniform OKLCH value with exact Lightness, Chroma, and Hue.
rgbToOklch.mathPath: The math path: RGB (0-255) → normalized sRGB (0-1) → linear RGB (gamma decode) → Oklab (LMS matrices) → OKLCH (cylindrical transform).
rgbToOklch.gamutTitle: Gamut Note: RGB is Always sRGB
rgbToOklch.gamutBody: Standard rgb() values are confined to the sRGB gamut by definition. Converting from RGB to OKLCH is therefore always gamut-safe — the resulting OKLCH value will never exceed sRGB boundaries. However, if you paste a color(display-p3 ...) value, the converter will detect the wider gamut and flag it accordingly.
rgbToOklch.faq1Q: Can I convert rgba() with alpha to OKLCH?
rgbToOklch.faq1A: Yes. rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5) converts to oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved as a slash parameter.
rgbToOklch.faq2Q: What is the difference between RGB and OKLCH?
rgbToOklch.faq2A: RGB is a device-dependent additive color model. OKLCH is a perceptually uniform color space where equal lightness values look equally bright. OKLCH makes it far easier to create accessible, consistent color systems.
rgbToOklch.faq3Q: Is RGB to OKLCH conversion reversible?
rgbToOklch.faq3A: Yes, for sRGB colors. Converting RGB → OKLCH → RGB yields the original values. The round-trip is lossless within the sRGB gamut.
rgbToOklch.faq4A: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively.
rgbToOklch.faq5Q: How do I use OKLCH in Tailwind CSS v4?
rgbToOklch.faq5A: Tailwind v4 uses OKLCH for its entire default palette. Define custom colors in your @theme block using --color-{name}: oklch(...) and Tailwind generates utilities automatically.

oklchToRgb.subtitle: Convert modern CSS OKLCH values into standard rgb(r, g, b) syntax for legacy CSS and canvas rendering contexts.
oklchToRgb.whyBody: When interfacing with legacy JavaScript libraries or 2D HTML Canvas graphics that lack native color space awareness, converting OKLCH to RGB strings is essential. Our engine applies exact matrix transformations through the Oklab LMS cone response matrices.
oklchToRgb.howTitle: How to Convert OKLCH to RGB
oklchToRgb.step1: Paste any oklch() value (e.g. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8)) into the input field above.
oklchToRgb.step2: Our engine converts the cylindrical OKLCH coordinates to Cartesian Oklab, then through the inverse LMS matrix to linear RGB.
oklchToRgb.step3: Linear RGB is gamma-encoded to sRGB and formatted as rgb(r, g, b) or rgba(r, g, b, a).
oklchToRgb.mathPath: The math path: OKLCH → Oklab (Cartesian) → linear RGB (inverse LMS matrix) → gamma-encoded sRGB → rgb() string.
oklchToRgb.gamutBody: When an OKLCH color falls outside the sRGB gamut (common with high-chroma cyans and greens), our engine automatically clamps chroma to the nearest in-gamut value while preserving hue and lightness. This ensures the RGB output is always valid and renders consistently across all displays.
oklchToRgb.p3Item: Display-P3 Colors: On wide-gamut monitors, the original OKLCH color appears more vivid. The RGB output represents the sRGB-clamped version.
oklchToRgb.alphaItem: Alpha Preservation: An OKLCH value with alpha converts to rgba(r, g, b, a) with the alpha channel intact.
oklchToRgb.faq1Q: Why do I need RGB if I have OKLCH?
oklchToRgb.faq1A: Legacy tools — canvas renderers, older JavaScript libraries, email clients, and some image editors — only understand RGB. Converting OKLCH to RGB ensures compatibility with these tools.
oklchToRgb.faq2Q: Is the OKLCH to RGB conversion lossy?
oklchToRgb.faq2A: For sRGB colors, the conversion is lossless. For Display-P3 colors, clamping to sRGB is a lossy step. The OKLCH original remains the source of truth.
oklchToRgb.faq3Q: Can I use OKLCH alpha in rgba()?
oklchToRgb.faq3A: Yes. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) converts to rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved.
oklchToRgb.faq4A: The engine clamps chroma to the nearest in-gamut value while preserving hue and lightness. You will see a gamut badge indicating the color was clamped.
oklchToRgb.faq5Q: How do I use RGB values in canvas?
oklchToRgb.faq5A: Pass the RGB string directly to ctx.fillStyle or ctx.strokeStyle. Canvas 2D only understands sRGB, so the RGB output is always canvas-safe.

hslToOklch.subtitle: Convert hsl(h, s%, l%) strings to CSS OKLCH format and eliminate non-uniform perceptual lightness distortion.
hslToOklch.flawBody: HSL calculates lightness as a crude geometric average of maximum and minimum RGB channels: (max(R,G,B) + min(R,G,B)) / 2. This ignores the biological reality of human eyes, which are 30 times more sensitive to green and yellow light than blue light. Converting to OKLCH solves this permanently.
hslToOklch.howTitle: How to Convert HSL to OKLCH
hslToOklch.step1: Paste any hsl() value (e.g. hsl(217, 91%, 60%)) into the input field above.
hslToOklch.step2: Our engine converts HSL to RGB, then applies gamma decoding to get linear RGB, then transforms through the Oklab LMS cone response matrices.
hslToOklch.step3: The result is a perceptually uniform OKLCH value where equal lightness looks equally bright across all hues.
hslToOklch.mathPath: The math path: HSL → RGB (cylindrical to Cartesian) → linear RGB (gamma decode) → Oklab (LMS matrices) → OKLCH (cylindrical transform).
hslToOklch.gamutTitle: Gamut Note: HSL is Always sRGB
hslToOklch.gamutBody: Standard hsl() values are confined to the sRGB gamut by definition. Converting from HSL to OKLCH is therefore always gamut-safe. However, the perceptual improvement is significant: HSL's uneven lightness means that hsl(60, 100%, 50%) (yellow) looks almost white while hsl(240, 100%, 50%) (blue) looks very dark, despite both having 50% lightness. OKLCH fixes this.
hslToOklch.faq1Question: What is the main difference between HSL and OKLCH?
hslToOklch.faq1Answer: HSL's lightness is not perceptually uniform — yellow at 50% lightness looks almost white, while blue at 50% looks dark. OKLCH's lightness is perceptually uniform: 50% lightness looks equally bright regardless of hue.
hslToOklch.faq2Question: Can I convert HSL with alpha to OKLCH?
hslToOklch.faq2Answer: Yes. hsla(217, 91%, 60%, 0.5) converts to oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved.
hslToOklch.faq3Question: Is HSL to OKLCH conversion reversible?
hslToOklch.faq3Answer: Yes, for sRGB colors. Converting HSL → OKLCH → HSL yields the original values. The round-trip is lossless within the sRGB gamut.
hslToOklch.faq4Question: Why should I switch from HSL to OKLCH?
hslToOklch.faq4Answer: OKLCH gives you perceptually uniform lightness, predictable palettes, and access to wide-gamut Display-P3 colors. It makes accessible, consistent color systems far easier to build.
hslToOklch.faq5Answer: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively.

oklchToHsl.whyBody: While modern front-end workflows embrace OKLCH, certain legacy CSS preprocessors, email clients, or native apps continue to mandate HSL formats. Our engine translates OKLCH into standard 360-degree HSL values with graceful gamut clamping.
oklchToHsl.howTitle: How to Convert OKLCH to HSL
oklchToHsl.step1: Paste any oklch() value (e.g. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8)) into the input field above.
oklchToHsl.step2: Our engine converts OKLCH to Oklab, then through the inverse LMS matrix to linear RGB, then gamma-encodes to sRGB.
oklchToHsl.step3: sRGB is converted to HSL cylindrical coordinates: hue (0-360), saturation (0-100%), lightness (0-100%).
oklchToHsl.mathPath: The math path: OKLCH → Oklab (Cartesian) → linear RGB (inverse LMS) → gamma-encoded sRGB → HSL (cylindrical transform).
oklchToHsl.gamutBody: When an OKLCH color falls outside the sRGB gamut, our engine automatically clamps chroma to the nearest in-gamut value while preserving hue. The resulting HSL value is always valid and renders consistently across all displays.
oklchToHsl.gamutLi1: Display-P3 Colors: On wide-gamut monitors, the original OKLCH color appears more vivid. The HSL output represents the sRGB-clamped version.
oklchToHsl.gamutLi2: Alpha Preservation: An OKLCH value with alpha converts to hsla(h, s%, l%, a) with the alpha channel intact.
oklchToHsl.faq1Question: Why do I need HSL if I have OKLCH?
oklchToHsl.faq1Answer: Legacy tools — email clients, older CSS preprocessors, native apps, and some design tools — only understand HSL. Converting OKLCH to HSL ensures compatibility with these tools.
oklchToHsl.faq2Question: Is the OKLCH to HSL conversion lossy?
oklchToHsl.faq2Answer: For sRGB colors, the conversion is lossless. For Display-P3 colors, clamping to sRGB is a lossy step. The OKLCH original remains the source of truth.
oklchToHsl.faq3Question: Can I use OKLCH alpha in hsla()?
oklchToHsl.faq3Answer: Yes. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) converts to hsla(217, 91%, 60%, 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved.
oklchToHsl.faq4Answer: The engine clamps chroma to the nearest in-gamut value while preserving hue. You will see a gamut badge indicating the color was clamped.
oklchToHsl.faq5Question: How do I use HSL values in email templates?
oklchToHsl.faq5Answer: Many email clients only support HSL or HEX. Use the HSL output directly in your inline styles — it will render consistently across email clients.

converterHub.subtitle: Six converters around one color space: move any web color into CSS oklch() notation, or move oklch() back out into HEX, RGB, or HSL. Pick your direction below.
converterHub.hexDetail: #3b82f6 from CSS, design tools, or color pickers
converterHub.rgbDetail: rgb(59 130 246) from legacy CSS or JavaScript
converterHub.toHexDetail: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8) when a tool only accepts HEX
converterHub.toRgbDetail: for canvas, WebGL, or any API taking 0-255 channels
converterHub.toHslDetail: for systems that still read hue-saturation-lightness
converterHub.tableTitle: The Same Colors in HEX, RGB, HSL and OKLCH
converterHub.tableIntro: Every row is one color written four ways. If you already know one notation, find your value in its column and read across to the oklch() equivalent — no single-purpose tool visit required.
converterHub.howItWorksBody: All six converters run the same core pipeline, just entered or exited at different points. Incoming colors are decoded into sRGB channel values, gamma-decoded to linear light, transformed through the Oklab cone-response matrices, and expressed as lightness (L), chroma (C), and hue (H) for oklch(). Conversions in the other direction reverse those exact steps. Because the transformations are deterministic math rather than a lookup table, converting a color to OKLCH and straight back returns the original value for any color inside the sRGB gamut.
converterHub.whichDir1: Writing new CSS or a Tailwind v4 theme? Convert into OKLCH. Once your values are oklch(), you can shift L or C independently to build scales and hover states without disturbing hue.
converterHub.whichDir2: Handing a color to a tool that only reads HEX? Convert out of OKLCH with the OKLCH to HEX converter. The result is the exact sRGB hex the color came from.
converterHub.whichDir3: Feeding canvas, WebGL, or a charting library? Use OKLCH to RGB — those APIs want 0-255 channel numbers, not a CSS string.
converterHub.whichDir4: Maintaining an older stylesheet built on HSL? Convert HSL to OKLCH to modernize values, or OKLCH to HSL when a legacy system has to keep parsing hue-saturation-lightness.
converterHub.gamutTitle: Gamut Notes Across All Six Converters
converterHub.gamut1: Into OKLCH is always safe. HEX, RGB, and HSL inputs are sRGB colors by definition, so their OKLCH results never need gamut clipping.
converterHub.gamut2: Out of OKLCH may clamp. OKLCH can describe colors wider than sRGB. When you convert an out-of-gamut oklch() value to HEX, RGB, or HSL, chroma is reduced to the nearest in-gamut color — the hue and lightness are preserved.
converterHub.gamut3: Alpha travels with the color. Transparency converts across every direction and lands in the standard CSS slash syntax, e.g. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5).
converterHub.faq1Answer: An OKLCH converter translates a color between CSS oklch() notation and another notation such as HEX, RGB, or HSL. It is useful whenever one end of your pipeline speaks perceptual OKLCH and the other end still speaks channel-based or legacy color formats.
converterHub.faq2Question: Is converting to OKLCH and back lossless?
converterHub.faq2Answer: Yes, for every sRGB color. The conversion pipeline is deterministic math with no rounding table behind it, so a HEX value round-trips to the identical 6-digit code. The one exception is converting an out-of-gamut oklch() value down to sRGB, where chroma must be clamped — by definition an approximation.
converterHub.faq3Question: Do browsers support oklch() without conversion?
converterHub.faq3Answer: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available in all major browsers since May 2023, so modern stylesheets can use it directly. Conversion is for the boundaries of your toolchain — exports, legacy systems, and APIs — not for the browser itself. See the MDN compatibility table for details.
converterHub.faq4Question: Does Tailwind CSS v4 need OKLCH conversion?
converterHub.faq4Answer: Tailwind v4 ships its default palette as OKLCH values, so custom colors defined in @theme can be written directly as oklch() with no conversion step. Use a converter only when your source values are still HEX, RGB, or HSL.
converterHub.faq5Question: What do the three OKLCH numbers mean?
converterHub.faq5Answer: Lightness (L) runs from 0% to 100% and behaves like perceptual brightness; Chroma (C) is saturation, starting at 0 for gray; Hue (H) is the angle in degrees around the color wheel. Keeping them in separate channels is what lets you adjust brightness without shifting the color.

tailwindV4.subtitle: Tailwind CSS v4 defines its entire default color palette in OKLCH instead of RGB. This guide covers what changed, how to write OKLCH colors in a v4 @theme block, and how to migrate custom colors from a v3 config without breaking class names.
tailwindV4.lastUpdated: Last updated: 2026-10-07 · Maintained by the OKLCH Colors team
tailwindV4.shortAnswerTitle: When Did Tailwind Start Using OKLCH?
tailwindV4.shortAnswerBody1: With Tailwind CSS v4.0, released January 22, 2025. The v4.0 release notes state: "We've upgraded the entire default color palette from rgb to oklch, taking advantage of the wider gamut to make the colors more vivid in places where we were previously limited by the sRGB color space."
tailwindV4.shortAnswerBody2: So from v4.0 onward, every value behind bg-blue-500, text-red-500 and the rest of the default palette is an oklch() color. v3.x and earlier stayed on RGB. The utility class names did not change — only the color notation underneath.
tailwindV4.sourceBlogLabel: Tailwind CSS — v4.0 release blog post
tailwindV4.whyBody: Two reasons, both stated in the release notes: wider gamut and perceptual structure. OKLCH is not confined to sRGB, so on wide-gamut Display-P3 displays the same color can render more vividly than its RGB definition ever allowed. And because lightness in OKLCH is perceptually uniform, a 500-to-600 step in the palette moves by a consistent amount of perceived brightness — the property that makes generated scales feel evenly spaced.
tailwindV4.whyList1: Same classes, richer output: no class renames — bg-emerald-500 keeps working, the value behind it changed notation.
tailwindV4.whyList2: Ready for wide gamut: when a v4 project lands on a P3 display, the palette can actually show the extra color.
tailwindV4.whyList3: Consistent lightness ramps: the 50–950 steps line up with perceptual brightness rather than channel math.
tailwindV4.themeBody1: Tailwind v4 moved configuration into CSS. Custom colors live in the @theme block under the --color-{name} namespace, and any value the browser accepts as a color — including oklch() — can be assigned:
tailwindV4.themeBody2: Because the token is an ordinary custom property, every downstream Tailwind feature — opacity modifiers like bg-brand-500/50, dark: variants, and color-mix() under the hood — operates on the OKLCH value directly. A HEX value still works in the same slot; writing oklch() simply keeps the whole theme in one color space.
tailwindV4.tableTitle: Familiar Palette Colors, Converted to OKLCH
tailwindV4.tableIntro: If you are carrying custom colors forward from v3, start from the value you already have. These well-known default-palette hex values are converted below by the same engine every converter on this site uses — copy the oklch() column straight into a v4 @theme block:
tailwindV4.tableCaption: The v3 column shows the published sRGB hex of each token; the v4 column is this site's build-time conversion of that same color.
tailwindV4.migrationBody: v4's upgrade guide covers the tooling side (the config moves from tailwind.config.js into CSS). For the colors themselves, the recipe is small and mechanical:
tailwindV4.migrationStep1: Move each color from the v3 theme.extend.colors entry into an @theme --color-{name} variable.
tailwindV4.migrationStep2: Convert the value with a converter (HEX → OKLCH, RGB → OKLCH, or HSL → OKLCH) and paste the oklch() result. Keeping the same name means no class changes anywhere.
tailwindV4.migrationStep3: Leave names that contain theme breakpoints or DEFAULT for a pass on their own — they map to slightly different variable patterns in v4.
tailwindV4.migrationStep4: Spot-check opacity modifiers: bg-brand/40 should still render — v4 resolves it through color-mix() regardless of the source notation.
tailwindV4.faq1Question: Does Tailwind CSS v4 use OKLCH for every color?
tailwindV4.faq1Answer: The entire default palette is defined in OKLCH as of v4.0. Your own colors can be any notation — Tailwind accepts HEX, RGB, HSL or OKLCH in @theme — but writing them as oklch() keeps one color space throughout the project.
tailwindV4.faq2Question: Do my class names change when I upgrade?
tailwindV4.faq2Answer: No. bg-blue-500 is still bg-blue-500; only the value behind it changed from an RGB to an OKLCH definition. Class renames in v4 come from other parts of the upgrade, not from the color-space switch.
tailwindV4.faq3Question: Can I still use HEX values in Tailwind v4?
tailwindV4.faq3Answer: Yes. HEX remains valid anywhere a color is accepted. Converting to OKLCH is optional — the benefit is perceptually uniform lightness for derived colors and gamut headroom, not a requirement for the framework to work.
tailwindV4.faq4Question: Do opacity modifiers work with OKLCH colors?
tailwindV4.faq4Answer: Yes. Utilities like bg-brand-500/50 work the same way regardless of the token's notation — v4 resolves opacity through color-mix(), which handles OKLCH values natively.
tailwindV4.faq5Question: Why do my v4 colors look slightly different on my new laptop?
tailwindV4.faq5Answer: If the display is wide-gamut (many recent laptops are), OKLCH colors can show more vivid reds, greens and blues than the same color rendered from its old RGB value on an sRGB screen. That headroom is exactly what the v4 release notes describe as the motivation for the switch.

vsHslRgb.subtitle: RGB describes how displays emit light, HSL rearranges that into hue-saturation-lightness for human convenience, and OKLCH models how humans actually see. This guide compares all three on the properties that decide real design work — and is honest about where the older notations still win.
vsHslRgb.lastUpdated: Last updated: 2026-10-07 · Maintained by the OKLCH Colors team
vsHslRgb.shortAnswerList1: Start new color systems in OKLCH. Perceptual uniformity means lightness, scales and contrast behave predictably, and the notation is future-proof (Baseline, wide-gamut-ready, Tailwind v4's default).
vsHslRgb.shortAnswerList2: Read HSL where you inherit it. It is serviceable for quick tweaks and still universal, but its lightness is unreliable — any automated scale built on it will drift.
vsHslRgb.shortAnswerList3: Keep RGB for the boundaries. Canvas, WebGL, image data and existing hex tokens speak RGB; convert at the edge rather than throughout your stylesheet.
vsHslRgb.comparisonTitle: OKLCH vs HSL vs RGB — Full Comparison
vsHslRgb.rowUniformityHsl: No — lightness is distorted per hue
vsHslRgb.rowDeriveOklch: Adjust L, keep C and H
vsHslRgb.rowDeriveHsl: Adjust L — but the result is not uniform
vsHslRgb.rowHomeRgb: Canvas APIs, device output, hex tokens
vsHslRgb.lightnessTitle: The Same Lightness Steps: HSL vs OKLCH
vsHslRgb.lightnessIntro: Both rows below walk the identical lightness values — 20, 35, 50, 65, 80 — for the same yellow hue. In OKLCH each step is a fixed perceptual increment, so the row reads as an evenly spaced ramp. In HSL the top steps crowd toward white while the bottom steps bunch into darkness, because HSL's lightness is channel math, not perception:
vsHslRgb.lightnessBody: The same trap appears at a single value: HSL hsl(60 100% 50%) yellow and hsl(240 100% 50%) blue both claim 50% lightness, yet one reads as near-white glare and the other as a deep dark. OKLCH resolves this — a color at 50% lightness carries the same perceived brightness whatever its hue, which is what makes it safe to generate palettes from numeric rules.
vsHslRgb.rgbDifferentTitle: Why RGB Is a Different Kind of Value
vsHslRgb.rgbDifferentBody: RGB is not a failed competitor — it is a different category. rgb(255 0 0) states how hard each channel drives on an sRGB display; it makes no claim about how bright or saturated the result looks, because that depends on the eye, not the signal. Two consequences follow:
vsHslRgb.rgbDifferentList1: "Lighter" has no channel. Making an RGB color lighter means raising all three numbers by an amount that differs per hue — which is exactly the guesswork HSL was invented to avoid, and OKLCH actually solves.
vsHslRgb.rgbDifferentList2: Interpolation is physical, not perceptual. An RGB gradient between saturated red and blue passes through a desaturated midpoint because channel math says so, not because the eye wants it.
vsHslRgb.hexRgbBody: HEX is RGB with different packaging — #ff0000 and rgb(255 0 0) are the same color. Every argument here about RGB applies equally to hex codes.
vsHslRgb.whenToStayTitle: When to Stay with HSL or RGB
vsHslRgb.whenToStayList1: Reading or writing APIs that demand RGB. Canvas getImageData, WebGL uniforms, and most charting libraries take 0-255 channels — convert OKLCH → RGB at that boundary.
vsHslRgb.whenToStayList2: Handing colors to tools that only parse hex. Design tokens in Figma plugins, older build pipelines, or brand guidelines fixed on hex values: keep the system in OKLCH, export HEX.
vsHslRgb.whenToStayList3: Small, hand-tuned one-offs. A single border color tweaked by eye does not need a color space argument — HSL's hue dial is quick and fine.
vsHslRgb.whenToStayList4: Auditing legacy code. When you cannot change a stylesheet, understanding HSL's distortions is enough to predict where its scales misbehave.
vsHslRgb.ruleOfThumbBody: The rule of thumb: keep your system OKLCH, convert at the edges. Every converter on this site exists for exactly those boundary crossings.
vsHslRgb.migrationTitle: Moving an Existing Palette to OKLCH
vsHslRgb.migrationStep1: Convert each base color to oklch() — the round trip is lossless for sRGB colors, so nothing visibly changes on day one.
vsHslRgb.migrationStep2: Rebuild shades from lightness steps instead of inherited hex values. This is where the improvement shows: equal L steps finally look equal.
vsHslRgb.migrationStep3: Re-check contrast with a real ratio — perceptual lightness makes WCAG results far more predictable, but always verify rather than assume.
vsHslRgb.migrationStep4: Leave RGB/HEX exports in place for tools that need them; they are derived artifacts now, not the source of truth.
vsHslRgb.faq1Question: Is OKLCH always better than HSL?
vsHslRgb.faq1Answer: For building and maintaining color systems, yes — perceptual uniformity fixes real defects in HSL's lightness. For quick hand tweaks or code that must speak HSL, the difference rarely matters. "Better" here means predictable under automation, not invalid.
vsHslRgb.faq2Answer: HSL derives lightness from RGB channel values rather than from vision: lightness is the midpoint between the strongest and weakest channel. Human brightness perception doesn't work that way, so equal HSL lightness numbers deliver very different perceived brightness across hues.
vsHslRgb.faq3Question: Do I lose colors by moving from RGB to OKLCH?
vsHslRgb.faq3Answer: No, going the other way can only expand: OKLCH encodes everything sRGB can (round-trips are lossless) plus colors beyond it. The one clamp happens converting a wide-gamut OKLCH value down to sRGB, where chroma is reduced to the nearest displayable color.
vsHslRgb.faq4Answer: Yes. Interpolating in OKLCH keeps lightness and chroma moving evenly, so a two-color ramp stays vivid through the midpoint. The equivalent RGB ramp desaturates in the middle because channel averaging pulls toward gray. Write linear-gradient(in oklch, ...) to get the perceptual path.
vsHslRgb.faq5Question: Which notation should new projects use?
vsHslRgb.faq5Answer: OKLCH for everything inside the design system, with RGB/HEX conversions only at tool boundaries. It is Baseline-supported, wide-gamut ready, and already the default palette notation of Tailwind CSS v4 — the direction the ecosystem is going.

palettes.intro: Curated 11-step (50–950) OKLCH color scales. Open any palette to copy individual values or save them into your design token cart.
palettes.whatBody: OKLCH colors are defined in a perceptually uniform color space that separates lightness (L), chroma (C), and hue (H). Unlike HSL, where 50% lightness looks completely different for yellow versus blue, OKLCH guarantees that equal lightness values look equally bright across all hues. This makes OKLCH ideal for building accessible, predictable color systems.
palettes.scaleBody1: Each palette is an 11-step scale from step 50 (lightest, near-white) to step 950 (darkest, near-black). The steps follow a perceptually uniform lightness curve: 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 950. Step 500 is the base color. Chroma is automatically tapered at extreme light and dark steps to keep every shade gamut-safe and visually clean.
palettes.scaleBody2: This is the same scale used by Tailwind CSS v4's default palette and by Radix Colors. It gives you a complete set of tints and shades for any UI role — backgrounds, borders, text, and interactive states.

generator.intro: Input any base color to automatically calculate an accessible 50–950 shade scale with optical lightness uniformity and gamut-safe chroma clipping — or build a custom palette of unrelated colors below it, where every color can be pasted in as text, changed in the color picker, or collected straight from the scale with one click on the swatch you like.
generator.howTitle: How Our Perceptual Scale Generator Works
generator.howBody: Traditional palette generators blindly interpolate HEX or RGB values, causing midtones to look muddy, hues to shift unexpectedly, and highlights to lose color purity. In contrast, our generator works directly within the 3D cylindrical coordinates of the OKLCH color space:
generator.step1Body: Maps lightness across 11 mathematically balanced steps from 97% (step 50) down to 13% (step 950), maintaining even visual steps between shades.
generator.step2Body: Calculates the maximum possible chroma allowed within the sRGB and Display-P3 gamuts for every individual lightness level, preventing harsh clipping artifacts.
generator.step3Body: Locks the hue angle exactly across all shade steps, eliminating the notorious "purple turning into pinkish-gray" bug seen in RGB generators.
generator.harmoniesTitle: Calculating Harmonies via Cylindrical Hue Angles
generator.harmoniesBody: Because OKLCH organizes colors along a continuous 360-degree cylindrical circle, generating complementary, triadic, and analogous palettes is achieved by exact mathematical angle rotations while preserving lightness and chroma constancy:
generator.compItem: Complementary: Hue angle + 180° for maximum visual contrast.
generator.triadicItem: Triadic: Hue angles ± 120° for vibrant, balanced triad schemes.
generator.analogousItem: Analogous: Hue angles ± 30° for smooth, adjacent gradients and tranquil UI accents.
generator.faq1Question: Can I build a palette of different colors instead of one color's scale?
generator.faq1Answer: Yes — the Custom palette panel under the harmonies. A 50–950 scale is one hue walked up and down in lightness, so all eleven steps are variations of the same color; a real brand palette is the opposite, and that is what this panel is for. Add a row, click its swatch to change it in the color picker, and type the variable name your own system already uses. Each row's value is a text field, so you can paste a color straight in — hex, rgb(), hsl() or oklch(), from a brand sheet, devtools, or the scale above — and press Enter; the row normalizes to the exact oklch() that will be copied. Copy all grabs the whole set as a Tailwind v4 @theme block, a :root block or JSON, and the preview above that button is character-for-character what lands on your clipboard. Two rows given the same name drop the second from the block instead of letting the browser silently pick a winner. Your palette — and the base colour the scale above is generated from — are stored in this browser, so both survive a refresh and a round trip through the picker.
generator.faq2Question: Can I export the generated scale directly into Tailwind CSS v4?
generator.faq2Answer: Yes! Type any variable name into the Variable field above (for example brand-accent) and click "Fill --color-brand-accent-*". The role is created on first use, so you never have to add it to the cart beforehand. Then visit the Export page to copy your complete Tailwind v4 @theme block.
generator.faq3Question: What happens when I click a swatch?
generator.faq3Answer: A small menu opens next to that swatch, so copying a single value and collecting it are separate choices instead of one guess. Pick Copy OKLCH or Copy hex to put the value on your clipboard, Save to variable to write it into --color-<your-name>-<step>, Copy and save to do both in one go, or Add to custom palette when you like that step and want it as a standalone --color-<name> variable in the panel below — the new row takes the color exactly as shown and drops the caret in its name field. Your cart is only ever rewritten when you choose one of the two save actions, and the same menu appears on every hue-harmony swatch. The Random button next to the presets throws a fresh in-gamut base colour to explore from.
generator.faq4Question: Why are extreme light and dark shades lower in chroma?
generator.faq4Answer: In human color perception and physics, as colors approach pure white (100% Lightness) or pure black (0% Lightness), the gamut triangle narrows to a point. Naturally tapering chroma at steps 50, 100, 900, and 950 produces clean, sophisticated UI tokens rather than harsh neon pastels.

preview.heroSubtitle: Preview your persistent cart roles live across real-world dummy UI components with WCAG 2.1 AA/AAA and APCA contrast scoring. Every coloured element is a token slot — click or right-click one to swap its colour. Each card has its own Dark/Light control, so one specimen can be flipped without touching the rest.
preview.wcagApcBody: While WCAG 2.1 uses a static mathematical ratio (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text), the modern Advanced Perceptual Contrast Algorithm (APCA) accounts for spatial frequency, font weight, and polarity (dark-on-light vs light-on-dark). Our preview tool evaluates your color tokens under both systems to guarantee accessible UI states in both dark and light modes.
preview.howToTitle: How to Use the UI Preview
preview.step1: Collect colors: Use the color picker or palette library to add colors to your cart. Each color is assigned to a semantic role (e.g. Primary, Danger, Success).
preview.step2: Preview live: The preview above shows your colors applied to real UI components — buttons, cards, badges, forms, and navigation bars.
preview.step3: Swap tokens: Click any colored element to open a popover where you can swap its color token, copy its value, or save it to a different role.
preview.step4: Check contrast: Each component displays its WCAG 2.1 and APCA contrast scores. Green scores pass AA; red scores need attention.
preview.step5: Toggle themes: Each card has its own Dark/Light control, so you can verify your colors work in both modes.
preview.sampleBody: When you export your colors, you get production-ready CSS custom properties. Here is an example of what a typical token set looks like:
preview.sampleNote: These tokens work with Tailwind CSS v4's @theme block and can be used directly in your CSS or JavaScript.
preview.scoringBody: The preview evaluates every text/background pair in your UI components. Here is how to read the scores:
preview.scoreWcagAa: WCAG 2.1 AA: Requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold).
preview.scoreWcagAaa: WCAG 2.1 AAA: Requires 7:1 for normal text and 4.5:1 for large text.

cssSyntax.intro: oklch() takes three values — Lightness, Chroma and Hue — optionally followed by a slash and an alpha value. This page is the complete syntax reference: what each slot accepts, how the parts interact, and the patterns that keep older browsers working.
cssSyntax.lastUpdated: Last updated: 2026-10-07 · Maintained by the OKLCH Colors team
cssSyntax.anatomyBody: The function has one required form and one optional addition — the alpha channel, which appears after a slash rather than as a fourth space-separated value:
cssSyntax.anatomyDiagram: oklch(Lightness Chroma Hue [/ Alpha])
cssSyntax.anatomyCode:
color: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8);
color: oklch(0.623 0.188 259.8);   /* decimal form — identical */
color: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.4);  /* with alpha */
color: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 40%); /* alpha as percent */
cssSyntax.anatomyNote: The three space-separated values must appear in exactly that order — L, then C, then H. There is no named-argument form and no default for any of them; a value that could not be parsed invalidates the whole declaration, which is why an unsupported or malformed oklch() line falls through to the previous declaration rather than rendering a broken color.
cssSyntax.cellLightnessRange: 0% (black) – 100% (white). 0.623 and 62.3% are the same value.
cssSyntax.cellChromaRange: 0 is neutral gray; saturation increases with the value. Typical sRGB colors sit between 0 and about 0.4.
cssSyntax.cellHueRange: 0–360° around the color wheel. Values wrap: 390 is the same hue as 30.
cssSyntax.lightnessNote: Lightness is a percentage or its decimal equivalent. 50% and 0.5 parse to the same lightness — the percentage form is the one you will read in documentation and the one this site's converters emit, because it maps directly onto the 0–100% scale the value is described in.
cssSyntax.chromaNote: Chroma is not a percentage of anything. It is an absolute distance from the neutral axis, so 0.1 in a dark color and 0.1 in a light color carry the same absolute colorfulness — but the dark color will look duller because low lightness limits how much chroma the eye resolves. The maximum chroma a lightness/hue pair can hold before leaving the sRGB gamut varies across the wheel; roughly 0.4 is the outer bound for sRGB.
cssSyntax.hueNote: Hue wraps, it does not clamp. oklch(70% 0.15 390) is perfectly valid and identical to oklch(70% 0.15 30). Negative hue values wrap the other direction. This matters in relative color syntax, where a calculation can easily push the angle past 360.
cssSyntax.alphaBody1: Transparency is the one optional part, and it always follows a slash. This matches the syntax rgb() and hsl() adopted in CSS Color Level 4, so an existing rgb(59 130 246 / 40%) converts to OKLCH by swapping the function name and the first three values:
cssSyntax.alphaBody2: Alpha compositing is unchanged from other color functions: two layers at 50% opacity stack to 75% coverage, and currentColor, inherit and custom-property substitution all behave the same way they do for any other color value.
cssSyntax.relativeBody1: With oklch(from ...) the function takes an existing color apart and rebuilds it channel by channel. Inside the brackets, the source color's own l, c and h are available as free values, which makes derived colors one line of CSS instead of a hand-computed second value:
cssSyntax.relativeBody2: This is the pattern behind most OKLCH design-system tricks — hover states, tonal ramps, and derived overlays — because it changes exactly one perceptual channel and leaves the others untouched. A HEX-based equivalent cannot do this: its channels do not map to perception, so "same color, a bit lighter" is guesswork.
cssSyntax.gradientsBody1: A gradient between two OKLCH colors does not automatically interpolate in OKLCH — you choose the space explicitly with the in keyword. Specify it and the ramp travels through perceptually even color, avoiding the gray, muddy midpoint that channel-by-channel RGB interpolation produces between saturated colors:
cssSyntax.gradientsBody2: The same in keyword works in conic-gradient(), in color-mix() (e.g. color-mix(in oklch, red 30%, blue)), and in the CSS transition of custom properties registered with @property — the four places where colors get blended.
cssSyntax.fallbacksBody1: oklch() is a Baseline feature (see browser support below), so fallbacks are belt-and-braces rather than daily necessity. Two patterns cover the remaining edge cases — a stale browser and a feature query for code that must not even ship when support is missing:
cssSyntax.fallbackStep1: 1. Cascade override — the browser picks the last declaration it understands:
cssSyntax.fallbackStep2: 2. @supports — gate everything OKLCH-specific, including derived rules:
cssSyntax.fallbackBody2: Because an unparsable color invalidates only its own declaration, pattern 1 works even when the fallback and the OKLCH value sit on the same property. Pattern 2 is the right tool when the OKLCH path also carries rules a legacy browser should not receive — relative color syntax, color-mix(), or wide-gamut gradients.
cssSyntax.outOfGamutBody1: OKLCH can describe colors that no sRGB screen can display. When a value falls outside the display's gamut, the browser maps it to the nearest displayable color: on an sRGB display the result is subtly compressed toward the edge of the gamut, while a wide-gamut Display-P3 display shows more of the original chroma. The syntax is the same either way — out-of-gamut is a rendering concern, not a parse error, so the declaration stays valid.
cssSyntax.outOfGamutBody2: If you need the exact in-gamut value before it ever reaches a browser — for a code review, a token file, or a tool that only reads HEX — clamp it with a converter rather than eyeballing it. Our OKLCH to HEX, OKLCH to RGB and OKLCH to HSL converters all reduce chroma to the nearest in-gamut color while preserving lightness and hue.
cssSyntax.browserSupportBody: oklch() is Baseline widely available: per MDN it has been supported across Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari since May 2023. Every syntax described on this page — including relative color syntax where supported, in oklch interpolation, and the slash alpha form — parses in current browsers.
cssSyntax.faq1Question: What is the correct order of values in oklch()?
cssSyntax.faq1Answer: Lightness first, Chroma second, Hue third — always space-separated — with an optional slash and alpha value at the end: oklch(L C H / A). There is no alternative ordering and no named parameters.
cssSyntax.faq2Question: Do lightness values have to be percentages?
cssSyntax.faq2Answer: No. oklch(0.623 0.188 259.8) and oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8) are identical — the number form is simply the same value written 0–1 instead of 0–100. The percentage form is more common in documentation because the scale is described in percent.
cssSyntax.faq3Question: How do I write transparency in oklch()?
cssSyntax.faq3Answer: Add a slash after the hue, then an alpha number or percentage: oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.4) or ... / 40%. The slash form is required — a fourth space-separated number is not valid syntax.
cssSyntax.faq4Question: Why does my oklch() declaration seem to do nothing?
cssSyntax.faq4Answer: An unparsable color invalidates only that declaration, so the browser falls back to the previous one (or the inherited value). Typical causes: a missing value, a comma instead of a space separator, or the alpha without its slash. Commas are the old CSS Color 3 syntax and are not accepted in oklch().
cssSyntax.faq5Question: Can I interpolate between two oklch() colors in a gradient?
cssSyntax.faq5Answer: Yes — state the interpolation space explicitly: linear-gradient(in oklch, ...). The same in oklch keyword works in color-mix() and conic gradients, and produces evenly spaced ramps without muddy midpoints.

about.subtitle: We're building the best free color tools for the modern web — powered by OKLCH, designed for accessibility, and built with love for the design and developer community.
about.missionBody1: We believe that working with color on the web should be intuitive, accessible, and enjoyable. For too long, designers and developers have struggled with color spaces that don't match human perception — HSL's uneven lightness, RGB's device dependency, and the muddy gradients that result from interpolating in the wrong color space.
about.missionBody2: OKLCH changes all of that. It's a perceptually uniform color space that makes it easy to create accessible, consistent, and beautiful color systems. Our mission is to make OKLCH accessible to everyone — not just color scientists — by building free, well-designed tools that handle the complexity for you.
about.builtIntro: OKLCH Color Tools is a comprehensive suite of free color tools for the modern web:
about.pickerBody: Interactive OKLCH picker with live L, C, H sliders, gamut detection, and one-click CSS export
about.generatorBody: Generate accessible 50-950 OKLCH color scales from any base color

about.exportBody: Export design tokens as Tailwind v4 @theme blocks, CSS custom properties, or stylesheets
about.whyIntro: OKLCH is a cylindrical representation of the Oklab color space, created by Björn Ottosson in 2020. It was designed to fix the perceptual flaws of existing color spaces:
about.whyList1: Perceptual uniformity: Equal lightness values look equally bright across all hues — something HSL cannot do
about.whyList2: Predictable palettes: Even lightness steps produce visually even color scales, making 50-950 systems trivial
about.whyList3: Wide gamut: OKLCH can describe Display-P3 colors that HSL and RGB cannot reach
about.whyList4: Smooth gradients: Interpolating in OKLCH avoids the muddy midtones of RGB interpolation
about.whyList5: Accessibility: Contrast ratios are more predictable because lightness is perceptually uniform
about.whyBody: When Tailwind CSS v4 moved its entire default palette to OKLCH in January 2025, it signaled that this is the future of color on the web. We're here to help the community make that transition.
about.value1Body: All of our tools are free to use, with no accounts, no paywalls, and no usage limits. We believe good tools should be accessible to everyone.
about.value2Body: All color processing happens in your browser. Your color data never leaves your device. We don't track you, and we don't sell data.
about.value3Body: Our code is open source. We document our methods, cite our sources, and welcome contributions from the community.
about.value4Body: We design for accessibility from the start — keyboard navigation, screen reader support, and color contrast that meets WCAG standards.
about.teamBody1: OKLCH Color Tools is built and maintained by a small team of designers and developers who are passionate about color, accessibility, and the open web. We're not a big company — we're a community-driven project that exists to make the web a more colorful place.

faqs.question: Are HEX to OKLCH conversions reversible without loss?
faqs.answer: Yes. Because sRGB is a mathematical subset of OKLCH, converting a HEX value into OKLCH and then back to HEX yields the exact original 6-digit hexadecimal code. The round-trip is lossless for all sRGB colors.

faqs.question: Can I paste 3-digit shorthand HEX codes?
faqs.answer: Yes! Our converter natively parses shorthand codes like #fff or #f00 and expands them correctly. Each digit is duplicated (#f00 → #ff0000) before conversion.

faqs.question: What is the difference between OKLCH and HEX?
faqs.answer: HEX is a device-dependent sRGB notation that mixes red, green, and blue channels. OKLCH is a perceptually uniform color space that separates lightness, chroma, and hue — making it far easier to create accessible, consistent color systems.

faqs.question: Do all modern browsers support CSS oklch()?
faqs.answer: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively. See the MDN browser compatibility table for details.

faqs.question: How do I use OKLCH in Tailwind CSS v4?
faqs.answer: Tailwind v4 uses OKLCH for its entire default palette. Define custom colors in your @theme block using --color-{name}: oklch(...) and Tailwind generates utilities like bg-{name} automatically.

faqs.question: What happens if my OKLCH color is in Display-P3?
faqs.answer: If the color exceeds sRGB boundaries, our engine alerts you with a Display-P3 badge and automatically provides the optimal clamped sRGB HEX code as a graceful fallback. The hue and lightness are preserved as closely as possible.

faqs.question: How do I export HEX fallbacks in CSS?
faqs.answer: On our Export page, switch to the "HEX Fallback + OKLCH" tab to generate twin variable lines, ensuring full backward compatibility on legacy browsers.

faqs.question: Is the OKLCH to HEX conversion lossy?
faqs.answer: For sRGB colors, the conversion is lossless — you get back the exact same HEX value. For Display-P3 colors, the conversion to HEX requires clamping to sRGB, which is a lossy step. The OKLCH original remains the source of truth.

faqs.question: Can I convert OKLCH with alpha to 8-digit HEX?
faqs.answer: Yes. An OKLCH value like oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) converts to #3b82f680 — the last two digits represent the alpha channel in hex.

faqs.question: Why does my HEX color look different on different screens?
faqs.answer: HEX values are absolute sRGB colors. On a wide-gamut Display-P3 monitor, the browser may render them more vividly than on a standard sRGB monitor. This is expected behavior — the HEX value itself does not change.

faqs.question: Can I convert rgba() with alpha to OKLCH?
faqs.answer: Yes. rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5) converts to oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved as a slash parameter.

faqs.question: What is the difference between RGB and OKLCH?
faqs.answer: RGB is a device-dependent additive color model. OKLCH is a perceptually uniform color space where equal lightness values look equally bright. OKLCH makes it far easier to create accessible, consistent color systems.

faqs.question: Is RGB to OKLCH conversion reversible?
faqs.answer: Yes, for sRGB colors. Converting RGB → OKLCH → RGB yields the original values. The round-trip is lossless within the sRGB gamut.

faqs.question: Do all browsers support oklch()?
faqs.answer: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively.

faqs.question: How do I use OKLCH in Tailwind CSS v4?
faqs.answer: Tailwind v4 uses OKLCH for its entire default palette. Define custom colors in your @theme block using --color-{name}: oklch(...) and Tailwind generates utilities automatically.

faqs.question: Why do I need RGB if I have OKLCH?
faqs.answer: Legacy tools — canvas renderers, older JavaScript libraries, email clients, and some image editors — only understand RGB. Converting OKLCH to RGB ensures compatibility with these tools.

faqs.question: Is the OKLCH to RGB conversion lossy?
faqs.answer: For sRGB colors, the conversion is lossless. For Display-P3 colors, clamping to sRGB is a lossy step. The OKLCH original remains the source of truth.

faqs.question: Can I use OKLCH alpha in rgba()?
faqs.answer: Yes. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) converts to rgba(59, 130, 246, 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved.

faqs.question: What happens with out-of-gamut colors?
faqs.answer: The engine clamps chroma to the nearest in-gamut value while preserving hue and lightness. You will see a gamut badge indicating the color was clamped.

faqs.question: How do I use RGB values in canvas?
faqs.answer: Pass the RGB string directly to ctx.fillStyle or ctx.strokeStyle. Canvas 2D only understands sRGB, so the RGB output is always canvas-safe.

faqs.question: What is the main difference between HSL and OKLCH?
faqs.answer: HSL's lightness is not perceptually uniform — yellow at 50% lightness looks almost white, while blue at 50% looks dark. OKLCH's lightness is perceptually uniform: 50% lightness looks equally bright regardless of hue.

faqs.question: Can I convert HSL with alpha to OKLCH?
faqs.answer: Yes. hsla(217, 91%, 60%, 0.5) converts to oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved.

faqs.question: Is HSL to OKLCH conversion reversible?
faqs.answer: Yes, for sRGB colors. Converting HSL → OKLCH → HSL yields the original values. The round-trip is lossless within the sRGB gamut.

faqs.question: Why should I switch from HSL to OKLCH?
faqs.answer: OKLCH gives you perceptually uniform lightness, predictable palettes, and access to wide-gamut Display-P3 colors. It makes accessible, consistent color systems far easier to build.

faqs.question: Do all browsers support oklch()?
faqs.answer: Yes. oklch() is a Baseline feature available across all modern browsers since May 2023. Chrome, Edge, Safari, and Firefox all support it natively.

faqs.question: Why do I need HSL if I have OKLCH?
faqs.answer: Legacy tools — email clients, older CSS preprocessors, native apps, and some design tools — only understand HSL. Converting OKLCH to HSL ensures compatibility with these tools.

faqs.question: Is the OKLCH to HSL conversion lossy?
faqs.answer: For sRGB colors, the conversion is lossless. For Display-P3 colors, clamping to sRGB is a lossy step. The OKLCH original remains the source of truth.

faqs.question: Can I use OKLCH alpha in hsla()?
faqs.answer: Yes. oklch(62.3% 0.188 259.8 / 0.5) converts to hsla(217, 91%, 60%, 0.5) — the alpha channel is preserved.

faqs.question: What happens with out-of-gamut colors?
faqs.answer: The engine clamps chroma to the nearest in-gamut value while preserving hue. You will see a gamut badge indicating the color was clamped.

faqs.question: How do I use HSL values in email templates?
faqs.answer: Many email clients only support HSL or HEX. Use the HSL output directly in your inline styles — it will render consistently across email clients.

faqs.question: What is the difference between OKLCH and HSL?
faqs.answer: HSL distorts perceived brightness: yellow at 50% lightness looks almost white, while blue at 50% lightness looks dark. OKLCH fixes this with mathematically modeled human visual perception, ensuring lightness is uniform regardless of hue.

faqs.question: Do all modern browsers support CSS oklch()?
faqs.answer: Yes! Chrome 111+, Safari 15.4+, Firefox 113+, and Edge 111+ support oklch() natively, representing over 93% global browser adoption.

faqs.question: How does the color cart work?
faqs.answer: Whenever you click "Add to Cart" or tap a swatch from our palettes, that exact single color is placed into your chosen UI role (e.g. Primary, Trusty Button, Danger). It automatically slots into the closest shade step (50–950), which you can then preview on real dummy UI components or export to Tailwind v4.

faqs.question: What does "sRGB" mean on the gamut badge?
faqs.answer: The color fits inside sRGB — the standard gamut that every screen, browser, and CSS color function can display. The badge's green dot means what you see on the canvas is exactly what the copied oklch() value will render: nothing is being clamped, so the swatch is a literal preview of the value.

faqs.question: What does "Display-P3" mean on the gamut badge?
faqs.answer: The color is more vivid than sRGB can reproduce, but still fits Display-P3 — the wider gamut used by modern phones, laptops, and monitors. Wide-gamut displays show it at full intensity; on older sRGB-only screens the browser gamut-maps it back toward sRGB, so it may look slightly less vivid there. It is a real, usable color — just one that benefits from a P3 display to appreciate fully.

faqs.question: What does "Clipped" mean on the gamut badge?
faqs.answer: The color is too saturated even for Display-P3, so no current screen can show it as authored — the browser clamps it to the nearest displayable color and the swatch becomes an approximation of your OKLCH values rather than the values themselves. Lower the Chroma slider (its max label shows the sRGB ceiling for that lightness and hue) until the badge reads sRGB or Display-P3 to get a color you can trust.
